cards.front: What is price elasticity of demand (PED)?
cards.back: % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price
Demand is price elastic: quantity demanded is very responsive to price
Number of substitutes, proportion of income, necessity vs luxury, time period, habit

cards.front: What is income elasticity of demand (YED)?
cards.back: % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income
A good with negative YED: demand falls as income rises

cards.front: What is cross elasticity of demand (XED)?
cards.back: % change in quantity demanded of good A ÷ % change in price of good B

cards.front: What is price elasticity of supply (PES)?
cards.back: % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price

cards.front: What causes a shift in the demand curve?
cards.back: Change in income, tastes, price of substitutes or complements, population, advertising

cards.front: What causes a movement along the supply curve?
cards.back: A change in the good's own price
The difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay
The difference between the price received and the minimum price producers would accept
A price ceiling set below equilibrium; causes excess demand / shortages
A price floor set above equilibrium, e.g. minimum wage; causes excess supply

cards.front: Effect of an indirect tax on a market
cards.back: Supply shifts left; price rises, quantity falls; burden shared depending on elasticity
When the free market leads to a misallocation of resources
A cost to a third party not paid by the producer or consumer, e.g. pollution
A benefit to a third party, e.g. education, vaccination
A good under-consumed in a free market because of information failure, e.g. healthcare
A good over-consumed in a free market, e.g. cigarettes
Non-rival and non-excludable, e.g. street lighting, national defence
People can benefit from a public good without paying, so the market will not provide it
One party in a transaction knows more than the other, e.g. used cars
When government intervention makes resource allocation worse
A tax equal to the external cost, to internalise a negative externality

cards.front: What are the four main macroeconomic objectives?
cards.back: Economic growth, low unemployment, low and stable inflation, balance of payments equilibrium
Gross Domestic Product: total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year
AD = C + I + G + (X − M)

cards.front: What shifts aggregate supply in the long run?
cards.back: Productivity, technology, labour force, education, infrastructure
Inflation caused by aggregate demand growing faster than aggregate supply
Inflation caused by rising costs of production, e.g. oil prices, wages

cards.front: How is inflation measured in the UK?
cards.back: Consumer Price Index (CPI), using a weighted basket of goods
Unemployment caused by a lack of aggregate demand in a recession
Unemployment from a mismatch of skills or location after industries decline
Short-term unemployment between jobs
An injection leads to a larger final increase in national income; k = 1/(1 − MPC)
Two consecutive quarters of negative economic growth
Short-run inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment
Use of interest rates and the money supply by the central bank to control inflation

cards.front: Who sets interest rates in the UK?
cards.back: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)

cards.front: What is the UK inflation target?
cards.back: 2% CPI
The central bank creates money to buy government bonds, lowering long-term interest rates
Use of government spending and taxation to influence aggregate demand
Government spending exceeds tax revenue in a year
The total accumulated borrowing of the government
Policies to increase long-run aggregate supply: education, deregulation, tax incentives
Government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment
A tax where the proportion paid rises as income rises, e.g. income tax
Many firms, identical products, no barriers to entry, perfect information; firms are price takers
A single firm with over 25% market share (legal) or the only seller (pure)
A market dominated by a few large firms that are interdependent
An industry where one firm can supply the market at lower cost than several, e.g. water
Obstacles that stop new firms entering a market: economies of scale, patents, brand loyalty
Firms agreeing to fix prices or output; illegal cartels

cards.front: What is the kinked demand curve?
cards.back: Oligopoly model explaining price rigidity
Analysis of strategic decision making between interdependent firms, e.g. the prisoners' dilemma
A market with low barriers to entry and exit, so the threat of new firms keeps prices low
Many firms, differentiated products, low barriers to entry, e.g. restaurants
